children.text: Every precision medicine intervention — from a targeted cancer therapy to a pharmacogenomic drug adjustment — begins with data. Biological data. The fundamental input is the sequence of nucleotide bases in a patient's DNA: adenine, thymine, cytosine, and guanine, arranged in approximately 6.4 billion base pairs across 46 chromosomes. Reading that sequence accurately, at speed and at scale, is the foundational technical challenge of the field.

The technology layer of precision medicine does not stop at the sequencer. It extends through a complex pipeline of computational tools, databases, AI algorithms, clinical decision support systems, and health information exchange networks. Understanding this stack — even at a conceptual level — is essential for anyone who will implement, interpret, or advocate for precision medicine in a clinical setting.
Types of Genomic Sequencing: Choosing the Right Tool

Not all genomic sequencing is the same. The appropriate sequencing approach depends on the clinical question being asked, the specimen type available, the turnaround time required, and the budget. Choosing the wrong test is a common and costly error — either missing a clinically relevant variant by sequencing too narrowly, or generating vast amounts of uninterpretable data by sequencing too broadly.

rows.left: Gene panel (e.g., 50-gene cancer panel) or single-gene test
rows.right: Whole exome sequencing (WES) or whole genome sequencing (WGS)

rows.left: Specific genes or variants known to be clinically relevant
rows.right: All ~20,000 protein-coding genes (WES) or entire genome (WGS)
$500–$5,000 depending on depth and clinical context
More uniform but lower depth across broader regions
High (may find variants with uncertain significance or unexpected diagnoses)

rows.left: Known mutation class, pharmacogenomics, confirmatory testing
rows.right: Rare disease diagnosis, research, comprehensive cancer profiling

body.title: Genomic Sequencing Types: A Clinical Comparison

children.text: Liquid biopsy: A minimally invasive test that detects tumor-derived DNA (circulating tumor DNA, or ctDNA) in a patient's blood rather than requiring a tissue biopsy. Liquid biopsies are particularly valuable for monitoring treatment response, detecting early relapse, and profiling tumors that are difficult to biopsy surgically. FDA-approved liquid biopsy tests include the Guardant360 CDx for non-small cell lung cancer. The test is performed on a standard blood draw.

Liquid biopsy represents one of the most significant recent advances in genomic testing accessibility. Traditional tissue biopsies require surgery or invasive procedures, specialized pathology processing, and adequate tumor material. A blood-based ctDNA test can be performed at any laboratory capable of standard blood processing. For Vermont's rural hospitals — where surgical biopsy capacity may be limited — liquid biopsy opens a practical pathway to companion diagnostic testing.

stats.context: A single whole-genome sequencing run generates approximately 200 gigabytes of raw read data before alignment and variant calling. (Illumina NovaSeq 6000 specifications, 2024)
stats.label: Raw data from one whole genome sequence

stats.context: A typical human genome contains 4–5 million single nucleotide variants compared to the reference genome. The clinical challenge is identifying the handful that are medically relevant. (1000 Genomes Project, 2015; gnomAD v4, 2023)
stats.label: Variants identified per human genome

stats.context: The FDA Table of Pharmacogenomic Biomarkers lists approximately 150 genomic biomarker-drug pairs with clinical relevance in FDA-approved drug labels as of early 2026. (FDA, 2026)
stats.label: FDA-approved genomic biomarker-drug pairs (2026)

body.title: The Scale of Genomic Data Generation

children.text: How Next-Generation Sequencing Works: A Non-Scientist's Guide

Next-generation sequencing (NGS) is the umbrella term for modern high-throughput DNA sequencing technologies that replaced the slower, single-strand Sanger sequencing of the original Human Genome Project. Rather than reading one DNA strand at a time, NGS instruments simultaneously read millions of short DNA fragments in parallel — dramatically increasing speed and reducing cost.

body.analogy: Imagine you have a single copy of a 3-billion-word book. Instead of reading it page by page, you shred thousands of identical copies of the book into millions of small confetti pieces — each piece containing about 150 words. A machine photographs every piece simultaneously. Then a computer algorithm uses overlapping words to reassemble the complete book, comparing each piece to a reference copy to spot any differences.
body.bridge: In NGS, the 'book' is your DNA, the 'confetti pieces' are short DNA fragments called reads (typically 150 base pairs long), the 'photographing' is fluorescent detection of chemical reactions as each base is read, and the 'reassembly' is performed by bioinformatics software that aligns reads to the human reference genome and identifies where your DNA differs.
body.concept: How next-generation sequencing reads the genome

steps.description: A biological specimen — blood, saliva, tumor tissue, or bone marrow — is collected. DNA is extracted and purified. Specimen quality and DNA quantity are assessed. Low-quality or degraded DNA (common in formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tumor tissue) can compromise results.
steps.title: Specimen Collection and DNA Extraction

steps.description: The extracted DNA is fragmented into short pieces and short synthetic DNA sequences called adapters are attached to each fragment end. These adapters allow fragments to bind to the sequencing chip and provide identifiers for bioinformatics processing.
steps.title: Library Preparation

steps.description: Each DNA fragment is amplified millions of times on the sequencing chip surface to generate enough signal for reliable detection. This creates dense clusters of identical DNA fragments at specific locations on the chip.
steps.title: Amplification (Clonal Amplification)

steps.description: The most common NGS chemistry (used by Illumina) reads DNA by incorporating fluorescently labeled nucleotides one base at a time. A camera captures the fluorescent signal at each cluster after each incorporation step, building a read of the sequence.
steps.title: Sequencing by Synthesis

steps.description: Instrument software converts the raw fluorescent signal intensity data into base calls (A, T, C, or G) with associated quality scores for each position. Output is a FASTQ file — a text file containing millions of short reads with quality information.
steps.title: Base Calling

body.title: The NGS Workflow: From Patient Tissue to Sequencing Data

children.text: Long-read sequencing technologies — from Pacific Biosciences (PacBio) and Oxford Nanopore Technologies — are increasingly used in clinical genomics. Rather than reading 150 base pairs at a time, long-read platforms generate reads of 10,000 to 100,000+ base pairs. This allows detection of complex structural variants, repeat expansions, and epigenetic modifications that short-read NGS misses. Long-read sequencing is now clinically validated for Huntington's disease, fragile X syndrome, and some rare congenital disorders.
The Bioinformatics Pipeline: From Raw Reads to Clinical Interpretation

Raw sequencing data — millions of short reads in a FASTQ file — means nothing clinically until it has been processed through a bioinformatics pipeline: a series of computational steps that align reads to a reference genome, identify variants, annotate their potential significance, and prioritize those most likely to be clinically relevant. This pipeline is where genomic data is transformed into clinical information.

The pipeline begins with quality control: reads that are too short, too low quality, or derived from contamination are filtered out. Clean reads are then aligned to the human reference genome (GRCh38 is the current standard) using alignment software such as BWA-MEM2 or DRAGEN. The alignment produces a BAM file — a compressed record of every read and its position in the reference genome.

Variant calling software then scans the aligned reads for positions where the patient's DNA differs from the reference: single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), small insertions or deletions (indels), and larger structural rearrangements. Each called variant is annotated against databases — ClinVar, gnomAD, dbSNP — to determine how commonly the variant appears in healthy populations and whether it has been previously reported in disease contexts.

ClinVar: A freely accessible public database maintained by the National Library of Medicine that aggregates information about genomic variants and their relationship to human health. Clinicians and laboratories submit interpretations of variants they have classified, building a crowdsourced knowledge base. As of 2026, ClinVar contains over 2 million variant submissions. However, the database has significant gaps — many rare variants have no ClinVar entry because they have never been reported in a clinical context.

stats.context: A 500-gene cancer panel may detect thousands of variants; bioinformatics filtering reduces these to ~50–200 candidates for manual review, and ultimately 10–30 clinically reportable variants. (Illumina TruSight Oncology 500 documentation, 2024)
stats.label: Variants filtered to clinically reportable range (per cancer panel)

stats.context: Modern cloud-based bioinformatics pipelines (AWS, Google Cloud, DNAnexus) can process a whole genome from FASTQ to variant call set in 2–5 hours. On-premise compute at small hospitals may take 12–24 hours. (DNAnexus, 2024)
stats.label: Bioinformatics pipeline runtime (per genome, cloud compute)

stats.context: An estimated 30–50% of variants identified by whole exome sequencing in a clinical context are classified as variants of uncertain significance (VUS), creating downstream clinical ambiguity. (ACMG, 2023)
stats.label: Proportion of WES variants classified as VUS

children.text: Variant Classification: The Interpretation Challenge

Once variants are identified and annotated, a clinical laboratory scientist or genomic medicine specialist must classify each one according to a five-tier system established by the American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG). This classification — not the sequencing itself — is where the most complex and consequential human judgment in genomic medicine occurs.

ACMG variant classification (five tiers): (1) Pathogenic — the variant causes the disease in question with strong evidence; (2) Likely pathogenic — high probability of disease causation, sufficient for clinical action; (3) Variant of Uncertain Significance (VUS) — evidence insufficient to classify as pathogenic or benign; (4) Likely benign — probably does not cause disease; (5) Benign — does not cause disease. Only pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants typically drive clinical management decisions. VUS results require disclosure but should not change clinical management without additional evidence. (ACMG/AMP, 2015; updated guidelines 2023)

The VUS problem is one of the most vexing issues in clinical genomics. A variant of uncertain significance (VUS) is exactly what it sounds like — a variant in DNA that has been detected but whose clinical meaning is unknown. It is neither clearly disease-causing nor clearly benign. For the patient and clinician, a VUS result feels like a weather forecast of '50% chance of rain' — technically informative, practically difficult to act on.

body.misconception: A VUS result means the patient has a dangerous genetic variant that should change their medical management.
body.reality: A VUS result means the clinical significance of a detected variant is currently unknown. Most VUSs are eventually reclassified as benign as more data accumulates. Clinical guidelines from ACMG and the National Society of Genetic Counselors explicitly state that VUS results should NOT be used to change clinical management — only pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants should drive treatment or surveillance decisions. However, patients and some clinicians misinterpret VUS as a warning sign, leading to unnecessary anxiety, additional testing, and sometimes unwarranted prophylactic interventions.

body.analogy: Imagine a forensic linguist is analyzing an old manuscript. They find a word that appears in no known dictionary and in no other historical text. The word might be a critical plot element, a scribal error, or an obscure regional dialect term. Until they find more manuscripts or historical context, they simply cannot know what it means — and a responsible scholar would not rewrite history based on a single uninterpreted word.
body.bridge: A VUS is a DNA sequence variant that appears in one patient but has not been observed enough times in disease contexts to determine whether it causes harm. Reclassification happens as databases like ClinVar accumulate reports from more laboratories. What is a VUS today may be reclassified as pathogenic or benign within 2–5 years as evidence accumulates — which is why genetic counselor follow-up is essential after any VUS result.

body.body: Ambry Genetics, a major clinical genomics laboratory, published a landmark study tracking the reclassification of VUSs in hereditary cancer genes (BRCA1, BRCA2, and others) over a 5-year period. Of VUSs identified between 2012–2017, approximately 38% were subsequently reclassified — and the vast majority were reclassified as benign or likely benign rather than pathogenic.
body.outcome: Findings reinforced clinical guidelines that VUS results should not drive preventive surgery or intensified surveillance, and demonstrated the critical importance of laboratory re-contact programs to notify patients of reclassifications.
body.source: Mersch J et al., 'Prevalence of Variant Reclassification Following Hereditary Cancer Genetic Testing,' JAMA 2018
body.title: Ambry Genetics: Tracking VUS Reclassification Over Time

children.text: AI and Machine Learning in Genomic Data Analysis

The scale of genomic data — millions of variants per patient, across hundreds of thousands of patients in research databases — is fundamentally beyond human capacity to analyze manually. Artificial intelligence and machine learning have become indispensable tools for pattern recognition in genomic data, enabling discoveries and clinical applications that would be impossible with traditional statistical methods.

In variant interpretation, machine learning models trained on databases of known pathogenic and benign variants can assign pathogenicity scores to novel VUSs — not replacing clinical classification, but providing a quantitative prior that guides human reviewers. Tools like AlphaMissense (DeepMind, 2023) used deep learning on protein structure to predict the functional impact of millions of missense variants with accuracy previously impossible at scale.

Polygenic risk scores (PRS) represent one of the most clinically significant AI applications in precision medicine. A PRS aggregates the effects of thousands to millions of common genetic variants — each individually contributing tiny risk — into a single numerical score that predicts an individual's genetic predisposition to complex diseases like coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes, or major depressive disorder. PRS are computed using GWAS (genome-wide association study) data and machine learning weighting algorithms.

Polygenic risk score (PRS): A numerical score calculated from an individual's genotype data that estimates their inherited risk for a complex disease based on the combined effect of many common genetic variants, each contributing a small amount of risk. Unlike single high-penetrance variants (e.g., BRCA1 mutations), PRS captures the aggregate of thousands of low-effect variants across the genome. A person in the top 5% of coronary artery disease PRS has a lifetime risk equivalent to carrying a familial hypercholesterolemia mutation. (Khera et al., Nature Genetics 2018)

stats.context: DeepMind's AlphaMissense (2023) classified 89% of human missense variants as likely pathogenic or likely benign with 90% accuracy compared to ClinVar-classified variants. (Cheng et al., Science 2023)
stats.label: AlphaMissense accuracy in predicting variant pathogenicity

stats.context: The tool scored all possible human missense variants (~71 million possible single amino acid changes) providing an AI prior for VUS interpretation at unprecedented scale. (DeepMind, 2023)
stats.label: Variants assessed by AlphaMissense

stats.context: AI-assisted phenotype-driven genomic analysis increased diagnostic yield in undiagnosed rare disease patients by approximately 3-fold compared to standard bioinformatics filtering in a 2024 study. (Rare Diseases Clinical Research Network, 2024)
stats.label: Improved diagnostic yield with AI-assisted rare disease analysis

body.title: AI in Genomic Medicine: Current Applications

children.text: EHR Integration: Making Genomic Data Clinical

A genomic variant result sitting in a PDF report is clinically inert — it cannot alert a prescribing physician that a patient is a CYP2D6 poor metabolizer when they write for codeine. It cannot flag an oncologist that a patient's new tumor biopsy shares a mutation with a trial for which they are enrolling. Genomic data must be integrated into the electronic health record to be actionable at the point of care.

EHR integration of genomic data faces several technical and institutional challenges. First, genomic results are complex structured data — not simply a number or a code — and standard EHR data models were not designed to represent them. Second, genomic data is lifelong and longitudinally relevant: a pharmacogenomic result from age 30 should still surface at the point of prescribing at age 70, even if the patient has changed health systems. Third, variant classifications change over time (the VUS reclassification problem), requiring EHR systems to support dynamic updating of stored genomic results.

EHR vendors — Epic, Oracle Cerner, MEDITECH — have developed genomics modules with varying sophistication. Epic's Genomics module, used by UVM Medical Center in Burlington, can store structured pharmacogenomic results and trigger clinical decision support (CDS) alerts when a patient with a relevant PGx variant is prescribed an affected drug. However, implementation requires significant clinical informatics build work and ongoing curation as drug-gene interaction evidence evolves.

Vermont context: UVM Medical Center uses Epic as its primary EHR. The hospital has implemented a pharmacogenomics CDS program that surfaces PGx alerts for clopidogrel (CYP2C19), codeine/tramadol (CYP2D6), and warfarin (CYP2C9/VKORC1). Critical access hospitals across Vermont using MEDITECH face a steeper climb — MEDITECH's genomics capabilities require third-party integrations and custom development that smaller facilities lack resources to implement.

body.body: Vanderbilt's PREDICT (Pharmacogenomic Resource for Enhanced Decisions in Care and Treatment) program, launched in 2010, pre-emptively genotyped patients and embedded PGx results into the Epic EHR before they were needed. When a physician prescribed an affected drug, a real-time CDS alert surfaced the patient's genotype and dosing recommendation. Over 14,000 patients were enrolled in the first phase.
body.outcome: CDS alerts fired appropriately in 96% of relevant prescribing encounters, and the program demonstrated that pre-emptive PGx testing with EHR integration was technically feasible and clinically effective at scale — a model replicated by over 60 health systems including UVM Medical Center.
body.source: Dunnenberger HM et al., 'Preemptive Clinical Pharmacogenomics Testing: Mayo-Vanderbilt Collaborative Research Program,' Mayo Clinic Proceedings 2015
body.title: Vanderbilt University Medical Center: PREDICT Program — First Large-Scale PGx EHR Integration

children.text: FHIR Genomics: The Interoperability Standard

HL7 FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is the dominant modern standard for exchanging healthcare data between systems. FHIR represents clinical data as structured 'resources' — Patient, Observation, MedicationRequest — that can be queried and exchanged via standard web APIs. The FHIR Genomics Implementation Guide extends the FHIR standard to represent genomic findings, variants, haplotypes, and pharmacogenomic implications in a structured, computable format.

The FHIR Genomics IG allows a genomic laboratory to return results not as a static PDF but as structured FHIR resources that can be ingested by any FHIR-compliant EHR — theoretically enabling true interoperability of genomic data across health systems. A patient's WES results generated at UVM Medical Center could, in a FHIR-enabled ecosystem, follow them to a community health center in Rutland, a rural critical access hospital in Newport, or a specialist at Dartmouth Hitchcock.

FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources): A standard developed by Health Level Seven International (HL7) for exchanging healthcare information electronically. FHIR uses modern web technologies (REST APIs, JSON, XML) to make health data exchange simpler than predecessor standards (HL7 v2, C-CDA). The 21st Century Cures Act (2016) mandated FHIR API adoption by all EHR certified for Medicare/Medicaid use — making FHIR the de facto interoperability standard for U.S. healthcare.

In practice, FHIR Genomics adoption is still early. Most clinical genomic laboratories return results as PDF reports. Few EHR systems have implemented FHIR Genomics ingestion workflows. And even where FHIR APIs exist, patient consent frameworks, laboratory accreditation requirements, and clinical data governance policies create friction. The standard is technically sound; the implementation ecosystem is still maturing.
Biobanks and Federated Learning: Building the Knowledge Base

The interpretive power of precision medicine depends on the depth of the reference databases used to classify variants and train AI models. Those databases are built from biobanks — large repositories of biological specimens (blood, tissue, saliva) linked to detailed clinical and phenotypic data. The UK Biobank (500,000 participants), the All of Us Research Program (1 million participants recruited in the U.S.), and the VA Million Veteran Program are among the largest.

Federated learning is an AI training approach that allows machine learning models to be trained across multiple data repositories without the underlying patient data ever leaving its home institution. Instead of centralizing data — which raises HIPAA concerns and patient trust issues — federated learning sends the model to each institution's data, trains locally, and aggregates only the model updates (not the data). This approach is increasingly used in genomic AI research to build models on diverse populations while protecting patient privacy.

Vermont has participated in the All of Us Research Program through recruitment at UVM Medical Center and Vermont community health centers. The program's diversity mandate — explicit recruitment of populations historically underrepresented in genomic research — is particularly relevant for Vermont, where the state's homogeneous demographic history means many common reference databases have limited applicability to its specific population's ancestral genetic background.
Digital Pathology and Imaging AI in Precision Medicine

Precision medicine is not exclusively about DNA sequencing. Digital pathology — the scanning of tissue biopsy slides at high resolution and analysis by computational algorithms — is an emerging precision medicine technology with significant clinical applications. AI models trained on millions of digitized pathology slides can detect subtle morphologic features that predict molecular characteristics, prognosis, or treatment response without requiring genomic sequencing.

Paige AI (FDA-cleared, 2021) and PathAI are among the leading digital pathology AI companies with clinical deployments. Paige's prostate cancer detection model demonstrated performance at or above expert pathologist level in large validation studies. Importantly, digital pathology AI can potentially be deployed at hospitals with pathologists who lack subspecialty oncology training — relevant for Vermont hospitals where recruitment of subspecialty pathologists is challenging.

body.misconception: AI in genomics and digital pathology will replace clinical specialists and reduce the need for genetic counselors.
body.reality: Current AI tools in genomics and pathology are designed to augment — not replace — clinical specialists. They assist with pattern recognition, variant prioritization, and quality control in tasks where human review of millions of data points is impractical. Clinical interpretation, communication of results to patients, integration with family history, and ethical decision-making about results disclosure require human genetic counselors and clinicians. The American Board of Genetic Counseling and ACMG have issued position statements affirming that AI tools do not constitute a substitute for trained genomic medicine professionals.

children.text: Technology Gaps in Rural and Resource-Limited Settings

The genomic technology stack described in this module — NGS instruments, high-performance compute clusters, bioinformatics pipelines, EHR genomics modules, FHIR-enabled data exchange — concentrates in academic medical centers and large health systems. Rural hospitals face a compounding set of technology barriers that are not simply about equipment cost.

Vermont's 14 critical access hospitals and numerous federally qualified health centers (FQHCs) illustrate the rural technology gap precisely. Most lack on-site NGS capacity — specimens are shipped to reference laboratories (typically Labcorp Genetics or Quest's genomics division), adding 7–21 days to result turnaround. EHR systems at rural Vermont facilities vary widely; several still operate on legacy MEDITECH systems without genomics module support. Broadband infrastructure gaps in northeastern Vermont further complicate cloud-based bioinformatics and telegenetics consultation.

The workforce gap compounds the technology gap. Genetic counselors — the clinical specialists who order, interpret, and communicate genomic test results — are concentrated in urban academic centers. Vermont has fewer than 30 licensed genetic counselors statewide, most employed at UVM Medical Center. Telegenetics — the delivery of genetic counseling services via video — has expanded access substantially, but requires reliable broadband that remains intermittent across Vermont's most rural communities.

Point-of-care genomics: Portable, low-cost sequencing devices — most notably Oxford Nanopore's MinION (the size of a USB drive) — are beginning to enable genomic sequencing in resource-limited settings. MinION-based sequencing has been deployed in rural clinics, infectious disease outbreak response, and even field settings. For Vermont, point-of-care NGS could eventually enable pharmacogenomic testing at community health centers without specimen shipment delays — though clinical-grade reporting infrastructure would still need development.

body.answer: The three biggest barriers and their practical solutions are: (1) Specimen processing and test access — the CHC lacks on-site genomic testing capability. Solution: Commercial reference labs (Genomind, Myriad Neuroscience, Tempus) offer buccal swab-based PGx test kits with prepaid shipping and 5–10 day turnaround. The CHC can order these like any reference lab test. (2) EHR integration — if the CHC uses a legacy EHR (MEDITECH, eClinicalWorks) without genomics modules, PGx results will return as PDF reports and cannot trigger CDS alerts. Solution: Results can be manually entered as structured data, or a third-party clinical decision support tool (e.g., First Databank Genomics, Translational Drug Development PGx CDS) can be integrated via API to surface alerts even in systems without native genomics modules. (3) Clinical interpretation — rural CHC prescribers may lack training in PGx interpretation. Solution: UVM Medical Center offers a telegenetics consultation service; the National Society of Genetic Counselors telehealth directory connects CHCs to remote genetic counselors. The Clinical Pharmacogenomics Implementation Consortium (CPIC) also publishes free, clinician-friendly dosing guidelines for all major PGx drug-gene pairs at cpicpgx.org.
body.hint: Think through the full pathway from ordering the test to receiving the result to acting on it in the EHR.
body.question: A community health center in rural Vermont wants to offer pharmacogenomic testing to its patients with chronic pain who are being prescribed opioids. What are the three biggest technology barriers they are likely to face, and what practical solutions exist for each?

children.text: The Health Information Exchange Layer

Health information exchange (HIE) refers to the electronic sharing of patient health information across organizational and system boundaries. Vermont was a pioneer in HIE through the Vermont Health Information Exchange (VHIE), operated by Vermont Information Technology Leaders (VITL). VITL connects EHR systems across Vermont's hospitals, physician practices, pharmacies, and long-term care facilities — providing a foundation for statewide genomic data exchange that most states lack.

However, VHIE's current genomic data exchange capability is limited. Standard HIE infrastructure handles administrative and clinical data (lab values, medications, diagnoses) — not the large, complex structured data objects required for genomic results. Extending Vermont's HIE to support genomic data exchange will require FHIR Genomics implementation at both the generating laboratories and the receiving EHR systems, along with updated patient consent frameworks that specifically address genomic data sharing.

body.answer: Traditional HL7 v2 interfaces exchange lab results as structured text messages (ORU^R01 messages) with fixed field positions designed for simple numeric results like a CBC or chemistry panel. A genomic result returned via HL7 v2 typically arrives as a PDF attachment or a series of text observations — readable by a human, but not computable or actionable by clinical decision support systems. FHIR APIs exchange data as web-accessible JSON or XML resources with formal data models for genomic observations, variant findings, and pharmacogenomic implications (as defined in the FHIR Genomics Implementation Guide). This matters for precision medicine in several ways: (1) FHIR genomic resources can trigger EHR CDS alerts automatically; (2) FHIR allows dynamic updating — when a laboratory reclassifies a VUS, the updated FHIR resource can propagate to all receiving EHRs without manual re-reporting; (3) FHIR APIs enable patient access — patients can retrieve their own genomic results via SMART on FHIR apps. For Vermont's HIE, migrating from HL7 v2 to FHIR for genomic lab result exchange is a prerequisite for true precision medicine integration at the point of care.
body.hint: Think about how each standard represents complex structured data, and what happens when a genomic result needs to be updated (e.g., a VUS is reclassified).
body.question: What is the difference between a FHIR API and a traditional HL7 v2 interface for exchanging genomic laboratory results, and why does this distinction matter for precision medicine implementation?

points: Genomic sequencing types range from targeted gene panels (focused, affordable, fast) to whole genome sequencing (comprehensive, data-intensive, complex) — and the right test depends on the clinical question, not just the technology available.

Next-generation sequencing reads the genome by fragmenting it into millions of short pieces, reading them in parallel, and reassembling the sequence computationally — a fundamentally different approach from the original single-strand Human Genome Project sequencing.

The bioinformatics pipeline transforms raw sequencing data through quality control, alignment, variant calling, annotation, and clinical classification — each step introducing analytical choices that affect the clinical result.

Variants of Uncertain Significance (VUS) are the central interpretation challenge in clinical genomics — they should not change clinical management and require follow-up as evidence accumulates toward reclassification.

AI and machine learning are transforming genomic data analysis through variant pathogenicity prediction, polygenic risk score computation, and digital pathology — but they augment rather than replace clinical genomics specialists.

EHR integration via FHIR Genomics standards is essential to make genomic data actionable at the point of care, but implementation lags significantly behind the technical capability of the standards themselves.

Rural settings like Vermont face a compounding technology gap — limited on-site sequencing, older EHR systems, bandwidth limitations, and workforce shortages — that requires deliberate policy and infrastructure investment to close.
body.title: Key Takeaways: The Genomic Technology Stack

learningObjectives: Distinguish the major types of genomic sequencing and explain when each is clinically appropriate
Describe how next-generation sequencing converts biological tissue into actionable variant data without requiring prior scientific training
Explain the bioinformatics pipeline from raw sequencing reads to clinical interpretation
Define variant classification categories and explain why variants of uncertain significance present a clinical challenge
Describe how AI and machine learning are applied to genomic data analysis, including polygenic risk scores
Explain the challenges of integrating genomic data into EHR systems and the role of standards like FHIR Genomics
Identify the specific technology gaps that limit precision medicine access in rural and resource-limited settings
summary: Modern precision medicine runs on a technology stack that most clinicians have never fully seen: from the sequencing machines that read DNA to the AI algorithms that interpret billions of data points, to the EHR integrations that surface results at the point of care. This module maps that stack from end to end — demystifying the biology, the computation, and the information infrastructure — and confronts the gaps that keep cutting-edge genomic technology out of reach for rural and resource-limited health systems like those across Vermont.
title: The Genomic Stack: Sequencing, AI, and the Digital Infrastructure of Precision Medicine
